title: Six Hundred and Fifty Miles on Foot: the Poet, the Brigadier, and the Sovereign Grand Commander
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Cobbler's Son and the Roads Out of Massachusetts

stops.name: Boston, the cobbler's second son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas gives 29 December 1809 at Boston
stops.campa: Benjamin Pike mends shoes and Sarah Andrews Pike keeps the house, and on the twenty-ninth of December one of their six children is born and named Albert. There is money for the district schools and no money for anything past them. The boy who will end his life owning a library of thousands of volumes, in four alphabets, begins with whatever sits on a cobbler's shelf in Boston. He leaves Massachusetts at twenty-one and comes back twice, once for a printer and once for a degree he does not sit an examination to get. Nothing in the town record marks the birth as different from any other that winter.
suggested_refs: The Boston of 1809, already staged in prince_hall.journey.json, where Prince Hall had been buried two years before Pike was born

stops.name: Newburyport, the schools of the north shore
stops.date_confidence: decade attested, year arbitrary for ordering; the sources name the towns and no dates. Byfield, a village of Newbury about eight kilometres southwest at roughly 42.7534, -70.9314, is grouped with Newburyport in the Encyclopedia of Arkansas and is not given its own pin here
stops.campa: He is put through the public schools of Newburyport, of Byfield nearby, and of Framingham inland, learning Latin and Greek from masters who take a poor and promising boy seriously enough to push him. The record of all three is thin: the towns are named, no schoolhouse is identified, no master, no anecdote. He will publish eight hundred and sixty-one pages of comparative religion and hand a copy to every man who takes the thirty-two degrees, and the languages that book runs on he gets for himself, without a master and outside any school. Hebrew first, then French and Spanish, and Sanskrit past seventy in Washington.
suggested_refs: The Newburyport, Byfield, and Framingham district schools of the 1820s
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Cambridge, the examination he passes and cannot pay for
stops.date_confidence: traditional; age sixteen is attested, the calendar year is inferred from a birth date of December 1809
stops.campa: At sixteen he passes Harvard's entrance examination and cannot afford the tuition, so he does not go. Harvard gives him an honorary Master of Arts in 1859, and accounts of his life have been converting that degree into an education he never received ever since. He teaches instead, at Newburyport, at Gloucester among the fishing boats, at Fairhaven across the harbor from the whaling fleet, because a schoolroom is the only paid work an unenrolled scholar can get. He is writing verse the whole time, and publishes Hymns to the Gods at about twenty-three.
suggested_refs: Harvard's 1859 honorary A.M. to Pike, routinely misread in later accounts as evidence of attendance
Hymns to the Gods, Pike's first published poem, c. 1832
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

segments.name: Fifteen Hundred Miles, Six Hundred and Fifty on Foot

stops.name: Independence, setting out with the traders
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by the TSHA Handbook of Texas; day defaulted
stops.campa: He reaches Independence on the Missouri, the assembly point where the Santa Fe caravans form up, and joins a company of traders and hunters bound for New Mexico. Mexico still holds the far end of the road. The men he travels with are freighting cloth and hardware down to Santa Fe and bringing silver and mules back. Pike is not one of them. He has no goods, no trade, and no stated reason for going; he is twenty-one, he owns a horse, and the company lets him ride out with it.
suggested_refs: The Santa Fe Trail caravan trade out of Independence, Missouri, 1831
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Taos, walking in after the horse breaks away
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month inferred from a March departure and a journey the TSHA describes as running about five hundred miles on foot
stops.campa: Somewhere on the plains his horse breaks away in a snowstorm and is not recovered. Pike walks the rest, some five hundred miles, into Taos. The Handbook of Texas puts more than half of his whole western journey under his own feet, roughly six hundred and fifty of about thirteen hundred miles. He comes into the town at the top of the Rio Grande valley on foot, a New England schoolmaster of twenty-one in ruined boots who has not eaten regularly in weeks, past adobe walls and burros and the irrigation ditch running down the middle of the street.
suggested_refs: The Taos of 1831, northern terminus of the New Mexican trade
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Santa Fe, a city of mud
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month inferred; the dismissive judgment on the town comes from his own later prose
stops.campa: Down the valley from Taos he comes to Santa Fe, capital of the Mexican province, and finds it beneath his expectations in every particular. He stays through the season, watches the trade, learns the country and some Spanish, and then attaches himself to a trapping party heading east onto the plains rather than going home. Three years later, printed at Boston in 1834, his judgment on the provincial capital of New Mexico reaches readers who have never seen an adobe wall. It is a city of mud.
suggested_refs: Prose Sketches and Poems Written in the Western Country (Boston, 1834), Pike's account of the Santa Fe country
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: The Caprock, trapping the Llano Estacado
stops.date_confidence: the expedition is attested by the TSHA; the coordinate is a representative point on the Caprock Escarpment and no documented camp or crossing site is known. Month set for ordering
stops.campa: The party goes out onto the Llano Estacado of West Texas after beaver and finds almost none. They cross the Caprock, the escarpment where the high plain drops several hundred feet in a single line of broken rock, and go on east into what is now Oklahoma. This is the ordeal at the center of Prose Sketches and Poems: no water, no game, no beaver, a country that gives nothing and is described in detail anyway. The book that comes out of it, Prose Sketches and Poems Written in the Western Country, is printed at Boston in 1834, and the Handbook of Texas calls it the first book dealing with the region between Fort Smith and Santa Fe.
suggested_refs: The Caprock Escarpment of the Llano Estacado, ground of the failed 1832 trapping venture
Prose Sketches and Poems Written in the Western Country (Boston, 1834)
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Belle Point, walking into Fort Smith
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the TSHA; month set for ordering. Coordinate corrected to Belle Point at the Poteau and Arkansas confluence
stops.campa: Separated from his expedition, Pike walks the last of it in and comes to the garrison post at Belle Point, where the Poteau runs into the Arkansas. Thirteen hundred miles behind him, six hundred and fifty of them on foot. He is twenty-two and has no money, no horse, and no employment of any kind. Arkansas Territory takes him in as a schoolteacher again, in a log building out at Van Buren, and there he begins writing up the country he has just walked across.
suggested_refs: Fort Smith National Historic Site at Belle Point, terminus of the western journey
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

segments.name: The Advocate, the Bar, and the Duel

stops.name: Little Rock, the Casca letters
stops.date_confidence: year attested; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: He writes a series of anonymous letters signed Casca, supporting Robert Crittenden for Congress, and they are good enough that the whole territory wants to know who wrote them. Charles Bertrand, who owns the Whig paper in Little Rock, finds out and hires him as associate editor. In October 1834 Pike marries Mary Ann Hamilton, whose family property is what lets him buy into the Arkansas Advocate and own it outright the following year. He writes about nearly everything in his life and about his wife almost nothing. The marriage leaves next to no record for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The Casca letters of 1833, printed anonymously in the Arkansas press
The Hamilton family property, source of Pike's capital in the Arkansas Advocate
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Little Rock, the Old State House and the first reports
stops.date_confidence: the reportership from 1836 is attested by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; the year of his admission to the bar is disputed between 1836 and 1837 and is not resolved here. Coordinate corrected to the Old State House at 300 West Markham, where the court sat
stops.campa: Pike becomes the first official reporter of the Arkansas Supreme Court and spends eight years making the state's case law usable: headnotes, reports, indexes, the machinery by which a decision becomes a precedent somebody can find. He sells the newspaper, and inside a decade is called one of the ablest attorneys in the Southwest. In 1840 the bank of a state four years old fails, and its broken credit is handed for winding up to a lawyer who walked into the territory eight years earlier with nothing. Whether he was licensed to practice in 1836 or in 1837 the sources do not agree, and neither of them produces a document.
suggested_refs: The Old State House, 300 West Markham Street, Little Rock, seat of the Arkansas Supreme Court in Pike's reportership
Pike's Arkansas Form Book (1842)
The receivership of the failed State Bank of Arkansas
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Buena Vista, the Little Rock Guards on the plateau
stops.date_confidence: attested; the battle is 22 to 23 February 1847. Pike was commissioned captain in June 1846 in an Arkansas MOUNTED INFANTRY regiment and discharged June 1847; the TSHA's looser wording, volunteer cavalry, is not adopted here. Coordinate corrected to La Angostura per the Battle of Buena Vista article
stops.campa: Pike helps raise the Little Rock Guards and takes them to Mexico as captain of Company E, in Archibald Yell's Arkansas regiment. At La Angostura, the narrows south of Saltillo, Santa Anna's army comes up against Taylor's line for two days. Pike's company is engaged in the plateau sector and he performs creditably enough that nobody disputes it. What he does dispute, loudly and in print once he is home, is the conduct of his own superiors over those two days. He is discharged in June 1847.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of La Angostura, twelve kilometres south of Saltillo, Coahuila
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: The sandbar below Fort Smith, the duel with Roane
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas gives 29 July 1847
stops.campa: Lieutenant Colonel John Selden Roane answers Pike's published criticism of the regiment's conduct at Buena Vista, and the two men meet on a sandbar in the Arkansas River near Fort Smith. They exchange several shots. Neither is hit. The seconds stop it and the men go home, and no prosecution follows, dueling being illegal and universally tolerated in the same breath. Roane will be governor of Arkansas within two years, and Pike will be back at Fort Smith on Confederate business fourteen years after this morning. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas gives the date, the place, and the outcome, and nothing of what either man said on the sandbar.
suggested_refs: The Arkansas River sandbar near Fort Smith, site of the Pike-Roane duel of 29 July 1847

stops.name: Washington, admitted before the Supreme Court
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; day and month defaulted. The coordinate is the Old Supreme Court Chamber in the Capitol, the Court's documented seat in 1849, not a Pike-specific address
stops.campa: Pike receives permission to practice before the Supreme Court of the United States. The admission opens the work that will occupy him for decades and make him rich: claims litigation on behalf of the Creek, the Choctaw, and the Chickasaw against the federal government, over money and land promised in treaties and not delivered. He is being paid by the nations to sue Washington, and he is still doing it twelve years later when a second government asks him to negotiate with them. The court he argues in sits in a low vaulted room in the basement of the Capitol.
suggested_refs: The Old Supreme Court Chamber, United States Capitol, seat of the Court in 1849

segments.name: The Degrees: Charleston, New Orleans, and the Supreme Council

stops.name: Little Rock, raised a Master Mason
stops.date_confidence: the 1850 raising is treated as established by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; the lodge, traditionally given as Western Star Lodge No. 2, is a traditional attribution the dossier itself declines to call documented. Day and month defaulted
stops.campa: At forty Pike takes the three degrees of the Blue Lodge, the ordinary Masonry practiced in every county seat in the country, and helps found St. Johns' College, a Masonic school in Arkansas, in the same year. What follows is not a hobby. Within a year he is organizing the Grand Chapter of Arkansas, within three he is its Grand High Priest, within nine he is head of an international body. The third degree he has just taken stages the legend of the murdered architect Hiram Abiff as a play, with the candidate laid out on the floor in the corpse's part.
suggested_refs: The Hiram Abiff legend as dramatized in the Master Mason degree, staged in hiram_abiff.journey.json
St. Johns' College, the Masonic institution Pike helped establish in Arkansas

stops.name: Charleston, Mackey communicates the degrees
stops.date_confidence: date and city well attested; the exact building is not identified and the coordinate is the canonical Charleston pin used elsewhere for the Supreme Council's seat
stops.campa: Albert Gallatin Mackey, physician, encyclopedist, and secretary of the Supreme Council, communicates to Pike the fourth through thirty-second degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite. It takes an afternoon. The Rite's mother council has sat at Charleston since 1801, and the degrees Mackey hands over are, by common admission inside the order, a ragged inheritance of eighteenth-century French material nobody has ever put in order. Pike will spend the next eighteen years rewriting every one of them. The thirty-third degree comes to him in Louisiana on 25 April 1857.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction, constituted at Charleston in 1801, a stop already staged in hiram_abiff.journey.json and prince_hall.journey.json
Mackey's Encyclopedia of Freemasonry (Washington, 1873)

stops.name: New Orleans, a charter for a railroad never built
stops.date_confidence: the New Orleans residence runs 1853 to 1857 per the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; 1855 is set midway for ordering
stops.campa: Pike moves his practice to New Orleans to push a railroad from the city to the Pacific. To qualify for the Louisiana bar he translates French legal material, the state's civil law being Napoleonic and not common law. He gets his charter out of the legislature. He never gets a mile of track. The transcontinental line is built after the war, from the north, by men with no interest in a Gulf terminus, and the charter stays on paper along with several other large projects of his.
suggested_refs: The Louisiana legislative charter for a New Orleans to Pacific railroad, obtained by Pike in the 1850s

stops.name: Philadelphia, walking out of the Know-Nothing convention
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; month set for ordering. The convention city is given as Philadelphia in the dossier chronology
stops.campa: The American Party, the Know-Nothings, meets in national convention and refuses to write a proslavery plank into its platform. Pike is a Whig by temperament, an anti-Democrat by habit, and a slaveholder by interest, and when the last national party that might have held North and South together declines to guarantee the last of those, he is finished with it. In five years he will write a secession pamphlet called State or Province? and take a commission from the government it argued for. He walks out of the hall with the Southern delegates.
suggested_refs: Pike's secession pamphlet State or Province? Bond or Free? (1861)

stops.name: Charleston, elected Sovereign Grand Commander
stops.date_confidence: date attested. The research pool's geography lens placed this election at Little Rock, which contradicts its own chronology lens and is rejected here: the Supreme Council's see was Charleston and no session at Little Rock is documented
stops.campa: John Henry Honour resigns and the Supreme Council elects Pike Sovereign Grand Commander of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction. He is forty-nine. He will hold the office for thirty-two years, until he dies in it, and in that time he rewrites the rituals, the constitutions, and the lectures of thirty degrees, moves the seat to Washington, and turns a small and disorderly society into an institution with a literature. Harvard gives him the honorary master's degree the same year.
stops.quote: In every age, its device has been, 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity,' with constitutional government, law, order, discipline, and subordination to legitimate authority, government and not anarchy.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447
suggested_refs: The Supreme Council, 33 degree, Southern Jurisdiction, whose Charleston seat is already staged in hiram_abiff.journey.json and prince_hall.journey.json
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: North Fork Town, the Creek treaty
stops.date_confidence: date attested by the University of Nebraska Confederate Indian Treaties portal, which confirms the treaty was consummated after Pike reached Fort Smith but gives no signing site; North Fork Town is the conventional location and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: The Arkansas secession convention names Pike commissioner to the Indian Territory and the Confederate government confirms him as commissioner of Indian affairs. He has been suing Washington on these nations' behalf for twelve years and knows which promises were broken and in what order. On the tenth of July he concludes the first of nine treaties, with the Creek Nation. The instrument offers what the United States has withheld: guaranteed title, delegates in the Confederate Congress, arrears of annuities paid in full.
suggested_refs: The nine Confederate treaties negotiated by Pike, indexed at the University of Nebraska Confederate Indian Treaties portal
sources: University of Nebraska, Confederate Indian Treaties portal
OK Historical Society Encyclopedia, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: The Leased District, the Comanche treaties
stops.date_confidence: the date of the two Comanche treaties is confirmed by the University of Nebraska portal, which names no place. The Antelope Hills attribution carried in the research pool is rejected: it is unsupported and its coordinate was seventy kilometres from the actual hills. The pin here is the Wichita Agency in the Leased District, the conventional placement, approximate and undocumented
stops.campa: On one day Pike concludes two separate treaties with Comanche bands, one with the Comanches of the reserve and one with the Comanches of the Prairies and Staked Plain, the same high country he crossed on foot after beaver thirty years earlier. The nine treaties in total run to the Creek, the Choctaw and Chickasaw jointly, the Seminole, the Osage, the Seneca and Seneca-Shawnee, the Quapaw, the Cherokee, and these two. Where he signed this pair the record does not say. The portal that holds the documents gives the date and leaves the place blank.
suggested_refs: The Wichita Agency in the Leased District, conventional but undocumented site of the Comanche negotiations
sources: University of Nebraska, Confederate Indian Treaties portal

stops.name: Tahlequah, John Ross signs
stops.date_confidence: attested; 7 October 1861
stops.campa: John Ross has held the Cherokee Nation neutral for six months and can hold it no longer. The Creeks and Choctaws have gone over, Stand Watie's faction is arming without him, and no Union force stands anywhere within reach. On the seventh of October he signs Pike's treaty at Tahlequah. Within two years Ross is in Washington repudiating it and the Cherokee national council has abolished slavery, while Watie fights on under Confederate colors to the end. The one document binds the nation and splits it. Whether Ross expected it to hold, nothing he wrote says.
suggested_refs: The Cherokee treaty of 7 October 1861, University of Nebraska Confederate Indian Treaties portal
sources: OK Historical Society Encyclopedia, entry 'Pike, Albert'
University of Nebraska, Confederate Indian Treaties portal

stops.name: Fort Davis, building on the Arkansas
stops.date_confidence: the commission is disputed: the Encyclopedia of Arkansas puts the brigadier generalcy in August 1861, the TSHA and Wikipedia on 22 November 1861. Neither is adopted over the other; the November date is used only to order the segment. The research pool placed Fort Davis in the Cherokee Nation, which is wrong: it stood on the south bank of the Arkansas about four kilometres northeast of present Muskogee, in Creek country, and the coordinate is corrected accordingly and remains approximate
stops.campa: Commissioned brigadier general and given command of the Department of Indian Territory, Pike withdraws from Fort Gibson and begins building a post of his own on the south bank of the Arkansas, near the mouth of the Verdigris. He is a lawyer of fifty-one who has never commanded anything larger than a company, in charge of a department made of nations he has just signed treaties with and cannot supply. Ordnance does not come. Pay does not come. He writes letters to Richmond about both and gets very little back.
suggested_refs: Fort Davis, Oklahoma, built by Pike in November 1861 near present Muskogee
sources: OK Historical Society Encyclopedia, entry 'Pike, Albert'
TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Foster's Farm, the scalps at Pea Ridge
stops.date_confidence: attested; Pike reached the field late on 6 March and the fighting described is on the 7th. The research pool's brigade composition is corrected: the American Battlefield Trust names the 1st Cherokee Mounted Rifles under Drew, the 2nd under Stand Watie, and Captain Otis G. Welch's Texas cavalry squadron of about a hundred men. No Choctaw, Chickasaw, or Creek regiment was engaged
stops.campa: About nine hundred men, two Cherokee regiments and a squadron of Texas cavalry, come onto the field late and go in at Leetown the next morning. Watie's men dismount and take a company of the 3rd Iowa Cavalry near Foster's Farm before Federal guns firing from Oberson's field break them into the woods, where they will not re-form. Pike has prohibited scalping in writing, and he court-martials a soldier for killing a wounded Federal, and the charge attaches to his name anyway, for the rest of his life and past the end of it. At least eight of the Iowa dead are found afterward scalped and mutilated. No eyewitness left a record of who did it.
suggested_refs: American Battlefield Trust, 'Cherokees at Pea Ridge'
Pea Ridge National Military Park, Leetown and Foster's Farm
sources: American Battlefield Trust, 'Cherokees at Pea Ridge'

stops.name: Warren, Texas, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: date attested by the TSHA; the coordinate is Warren in Tyler County, Texas, and the identification of that Warren with the arrest site is not independently confirmed. Pike's resignation, tendered 12 July 1862 over General Hindman's orders sending Indian Territory troops outside the Territory, is accepted the same November
stops.campa: Pike resigns in July over Thomas Hindman's orders moving Indian Territory troops out of the Territory, which he holds to be a breach of the treaties he himself wrote. He publishes his objections. Confederate authority arrests him at Warren, Texas, on charges built out of the Pea Ridge allegations and the command dispute, then drops them, accepts the resignation, and lets him go. Nineteen months as a Confederate officer, nine treaties, one post, one battle, and a court-martial he brought against his own side. He goes back to Arkansas.
suggested_refs: Pike's letter of resignation of 12 July 1862 and his published protest against General Hindman
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'
OK Historical Society Encyclopedia, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Greasy Cove, the retreat into the mountains
stops.date_confidence: the withdrawal to southern Arkansas is attested by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas and placed at Greasy Cove, Montgomery County; the coordinate is approximate for that vicinity. The afterlife lens of the research pool put Greasy Cove forty-five kilometres away in Pike or Howard County, and that placement is rejected in favor of Montgomery County. Month set for ordering
stops.campa: He goes to ground in the Ouachitas, in a hollow called Greasy Cove, with his books. In 1864 he surfaces long enough to sit as an associate justice on the Confederate-aligned Arkansas Supreme Court, and then goes back. Local tradition adds a trunk of gold, jayhawkers who raid the camp and scatter his library across the ground, and a night when he swims the Little Missouri River holding the manuscript of Morals and Dogma clear of the water. The withdrawal is documented. None of the rest is; no letter, memoir, or newspaper of the period carries any of it, and the book was not published until 1871.
suggested_refs: The Greasy Cove and Little Missouri traditions in Arkansas local history and Masonic retellings, both flagged in the research dossier as legend without early attestation

segments.name: The Pardon and the Memphis Editorial

stops.name: Washington, the pardon from Andrew Johnson
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict and are not reconciled here. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas and the TSHA both give presidential amnesty on 30 August 1865; Wikipedia, following Walter Lee Brown's biography, has Pike applying to Johnson on 24 June 1865 and pardoned on 23 April 1866. The 1865 date is used only for ordering
stops.campa: With the surrender Pike goes to New York and then over the border into Canada, expecting arrest as a former Confederate general and as the officer of Pea Ridge. Andrew Johnson pardons him. A brigadier who signed nine treaties for the losing side walks out of the war free and opens a law practice. The nations who signed those treaties get nothing comparable. Whether the pardon comes in August 1865 or in April 1866 depends on the authority consulted: two state encyclopedias give the earlier date, and his modern biographer has the application going in that June and the pardon coming back the following spring. Nobody has reconciled them.
suggested_refs: Walter Lee Brown, A Life of Albert Pike (1997), on the pardon chronology
The Confederate exile communities in Canada, 1865
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Memphis, the Daily Appeal and the Southern Brotherhood
stops.date_confidence: the editorial of 16 April 1868 is attested. The claim that Pike held Klan office is tagged as tradition, not fact: it traces to Walter L. Fleming's 1905 republication of John C. Lester's 1884 reminiscences, to Susan Lawrence Davis (1924) and Stanley Horn (1939), and no contemporaneous membership record, appointment, or the Klan's own 1868 Prescript names him
stops.campa: Pike settles in Memphis, practices law with the former Confederate general Charles W. Adams, and edits the Memphis Daily Appeal against Congressional Reconstruction and against Black suffrage. From an editorial he prints on the sixteenth of April, and from books written thirty-seven and fifty-six years later, comes the durable claim that Nathan Bedford Forrest made him the Klan's chief judicial officer. No document of the period says so, and his modern biographer does not believe it. What the editorial itself calls for is a secret association of Southern white men for their own defense. It names no organization.
suggested_refs: freemasonry.bcy.ca, 'Albert Pike and the KKK', tracing the tradition to Fleming (1905) and Davis (1924)
Walter Lee Brown, A Life of Albert Pike (1997)

stops.name: Washington, the Supreme Council on Third Street
stops.date_confidence: the permanent move to Washington in 1870 is attested; day and month defaulted. The coordinate is an approximate placement near the pre-1915 Supreme Council premises on Third Street NW cited in Scottish Rite institutional histories, not a verified street address. The present House of the Temple on 16th Street was not built until after Pike's death
stops.campa: Pike moves to Washington for good and lives in the Supreme Council's building, which is not the marble thing tourists photograph on 16th Street; that was built two decades after he died. He edits the Democratic Patriot, practices law with the former senator Robert Ward Johnson until about 1880, and in 1874 backs Elisha Baxter's claim to the Arkansas governorship through the Brooks-Baxter fight. He is sixty, and everything he is now remembered for comes out of the twenty years he spends in these rooms with his library. No source reached gives their street address.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Council's Third Street NW premises, Pike's residence and workplace 1870 to 1891
The Brooks-Baxter War of 1874 and the Old State House at Little Rock

stops.name: Washington, Morals and Dogma comes off the press
stops.date_confidence: year attested; day and month defaulted
stops.campa: Eight hundred and sixty-one pages, one lecture for each of the thirty-two degrees, published by the Supreme Council and given to every man who takes them. It runs through the Kabbalah, the Vedas, Zoroaster, the Gnostics, Hermetic writing, and the Mysteries, treating all of them as symbolic repositories of one thing. For ninety-eight years every new member of the Southern Jurisdiction receives a copy. Most do not read it. Those who do are told on the first page that they are free to reject and dissent from whatever in it strikes them as untrue or unsound.
stops.quote: Force, unregulated or ill-regulated, is not only wasted in the void, like that of gunpowder burned in the open air, and steam unconfined by science; but, striking in the dark, and its blows meeting only the air, they recoil and bruise itself.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, opening of the First Degree lecture
suggested_refs: Morals and Dogma of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry (Charleston, 1871), the edition staged in hiram_abiff.journey.json
sources: TSHA Handbook of Texas, entry 'Pike, Albert'

stops.name: Washington, the preface that gives the book away
stops.date_confidence: same publication year as the volume; the month is set only to place this stop after the book's appearance in the segment
stops.campa: In his own preface Pike says he has not troubled to separate what he wrote from what he took. It is a startling admission for a book of eight hundred pages and it turns out to be exact. Long passages are translated, unmarked, out of Eliphas Levi, the French occultist whose name does not appear once in the volume. Arturo de Hoyos, the Rite's own archivist, spends years tracing the borrowings and prints them in the margins of an annotated edition published a hundred and forty years after the first.
stops.quote: He claims, therefore, little of the merit of authorship, and has not cared to distinguish his own from that which he has taken from other sources, being quite willing that every portion of the book, in turn, may be regarded as borrowed from some old and better writer.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, Preface
suggested_refs: Arturo de Hoyos, ed., Albert Pike's Morals and Dogma: Annotated Edition (2011), tracing the unattributed sources
arthur_edward_waite.journey.json, 'British Museum Reading Room, the finding of Eliphas Levi' (1881)
sources: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma, Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, Preface

stops.name: Washington, the Blue Degrees and the Sphinx
stops.date_confidence: the passage stands in Chapter XXX, Knight Kadosh, of the 1871 volume; the month here orders the stop within the segment and is not an event date. The research pool suggested this bracketed passage might be compiled rather than Pike's own; in this chapter Pike's typography is consistent, borrowed Levi material sits in quotation marks and his own interpolations in square brackets, and three other bracketed insertions in the same pages follow the rule. It is his voice
stops.campa: In the thirtieth degree Pike writes that the ordinary Mason is deliberately misled, that the symbols of the first three degrees are given to him with false interpretations, and that the true explanation is kept for the adepts. It is the single most quoted sentence he ever wrote and it is quoted almost exclusively by people accusing Masonry of exactly what it says. He puts it in a book he then hands to every candidate. The brackets around it are his own and so is the claim: in the same few pages the material he is translating out of Eliphas Levi sits inside quotation marks, and three other bracketed insertions follow the same rule.
stops.quote: [The Blue Degrees are but the outer court or portico of the Temple. Part of the symbols are displayed there to the Initiate, but he is intentionally misled by false interpretations. It is not intended that he shall understand them; but it is intended that he shall imagine he understands them. Their true explication is reserved for the Adepts, the Princes of Masonry... Masonry is the veritable Sphinx, buried to the head in the sands heaped round it by the ages.]
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, Ch. XXX, Knight Kadosh; brackets in the original

stops.name: Washington, the nineteenth degree and the word Lucifer
stops.date_confidence: the passage stands in the nineteenth degree lecture of the 1871 volume; the month orders the stop and is not an event date
stops.campa: Discussing the Apocalypse in the nineteenth degree, Pike takes up the name Lucifer in its plain Latin sense, light-bearer, son of the morning, and asks how such a name came to belong to the spirit of darkness. It is a philological point made in a book full of philological points. Extracted from its paragraph and set on its own it reads as an avowal, which is precisely how a French pamphleteer uses it twenty years later, and how a great deal of the twentieth century goes on using it after that pamphleteer has confessed in public. The paragraph it comes out of is about the antiquity of revelation.
stops.quote: LUCIFER, the Light-bearer! Strange and mysterious name to give to the Spirit of Darkness! Lucifer, the Son of the Morning! Is it he who bears the Light, and with its splendors intolerable blinds feeble, sensual, or selfish Souls? Doubt it not! for traditions are full of Divine Revelations and Inspirations: and Inspiration is not of one Age nor of one Creed.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, 19th Degree lecture, on the Apocalypse
suggested_refs: The nineteenth degree lecture of Morals and Dogma, source of the passage weaponized by the Taxil hoax

stops.name: Washington, the contradiction he does not resolve
stops.date_confidence: both passages stand in the 1871 volume, the first in Chapter X, Illustrious Elect of the Fifteen, in the discussion of religious persecution; the month orders the stop and is not an event date
stops.campa: In the tenth degree Pike writes that Masonry is not a religion and that a man who makes a religious belief of it falsifies it. Elsewhere in the same book he writes that every Masonic lodge is a temple of religion and its teachings are instruction in religion. He never reconciles the two, never notes the collision, and gives the volume to men who will read both sentences inside a year. Part of this is the compiler's problem: a book made of other men's paragraphs inherits their disagreements. Where the rest of it comes from the book does not say.
stops.quote: Masonry is not a religion. He who makes of it a religious belief, falsifies and denaturalizes it.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447, Ch. X, Illustrious Elect of the Fifteen
suggested_refs: The counter-passage in the same volume: 'Every Masonic Lodge is a temple of religion; and its teachings are instruction in religion.'

stops.name: Washington, toleration written by a Confederate
stops.date_confidence: the passage stands in the 1871 volume; the month orders the stop and is not an event date. The reading of the closing clause as a reference to the Union's prosecution of the war is an inference from the wording and from Pike's own service, not an authorial statement
stops.campa: Pike writes that Masonry alone preaches toleration and rebukes three things: the monarch who conquers, the church that burns heretics, and the confederation of states that insists on holding a union together by force. He is six years out of a war in which he wore the other side's stars. The sentence is doing two jobs at once, one of them universal and one of them local. Nothing in the paragraph tells a reader in Ohio in 1872 that the second job is there at all.
stops.quote: Masonry alone preaches Toleration, the right of man to abide by his own faith, the right of all States to govern themselves. It rebukes alike the monarch who seeks to extend his dominions by conquest, the Church that claims the right to repress heresy by fire and steel, and the confederation of States that insist on maintaining a union by force and restoring brotherhood by slaughter and subjugation.
stops.quote_source: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma (1871), Project Gutenberg ed. #19447
suggested_refs: Morals and Dogma, published six years after Pike's Confederate service ended

stops.name: Washington, Sanskrit at seventy
stops.date_confidence: the late-life Sanskrit study is attested by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas without a start date; 1880 is set for ordering. The posthumous publication details, a limited 1930 edition edited by Marshall W. Wood, come from the research dossier and were not confirmed against a library catalogue record
stops.campa: In his seventies Pike learns Sanskrit and goes at the Rig-Veda directly, producing thousands of manuscript pages on the Aryan gods and their worship. None of it is published while he lives. Some appears in 1930 in a small edition; more comes out in the 2000s when the Rite's archivist starts working through the papers. It is the same method as Morals and Dogma applied to a single source, by an old man who has stopped needing an audience for it. The 1930 edition is credited to Marshall W. Wood and has not been checked here against a catalogue record.

stops.name: Washington, the rituals given to Thornton Jackson
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the transmission is dated to Pike's late years by the research dossier citing Arturo de Hoyos, 'On the Origins of the Prince Hall Scottish Rite Rituals,' Heredom 5 (1996). The specific year is set for ordering and is not attested
stops.campa: Thornton A. Jackson is Sovereign Grand Commander of the United Supreme Council, the Prince Hall body, and Pike gives him a complete set of the Scottish Rite rituals he spent eighteen years rewriting. He also refuses, in writing, to recognize Black Masons as his brothers. Both things are him. The lineage running back to Prince Hall's African Lodge in Boston, chartered in 1784 out of London because no American lodge would have it, takes its working degrees from a man who will not sit with its officers as equals. De Hoyos dates the transmission no more closely than to Pike's last years.

stops.name: Washington, death at the Supreme Council
stops.date_confidence: attested; 2 April 1891, aged 81. The afterlife lens of the research pool pinned this death at 38.9072, -77.0369, which is the 16th Street corridor near a building that did not exist in 1891; the Third Street premises are used here instead
stops.campa: He dies in the building he had run for thirty-two years, eighty-one years old, six feet and more of him and long white hair to the shoulders. The reported cause is a progressive obstruction of the esophagus that stopped him eating and then stopped him drinking. No diagnosis survives and no autopsy was made, so what is known of how Albert Pike died is only what the people around the bed described: a man starving over weeks in a room full of his own books, in four alphabets, that he can no longer get up to read.

stops.name: Oak Hill Cemetery, buried against his instructions
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Oak Hill in 1891 is attested; the exact day of interment is not recorded in the reachable sources and the sixth is a placeholder for ordering. The cremation request and the acacia detail are dossier-sourced and were not independently confirmed; Oak Hill's own reference material does not mention Pike
stops.campa: He had asked to be cremated and his ashes scattered under the acacia trees at the Supreme Council's home. The acacia is the plant that marks the grave in the legend of Hiram Abiff, the sprig by which the searchers find the murdered architect, and Pike had rewritten that degree with his own hands. They bury him instead, at Oak Hill in Georgetown, in the ground, with full Masonic rites and a long procession of the order he had headed for thirty-two years. It is the only instruction he is known to have left about his own body. The day of the interment is not recorded anywhere reachable, and Oak Hill's own reference material does not mention him.

stops.name: Charleston, the letter with no catalogue number
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of a fabrication. The Pike to Mazzini letter of 15 August 1871 has no catalogue number, no manuscript image, and no chain of custody at the British Museum or Library where it was long said to sit; its three-war script postdates the events it claims to foretell and it appears in no authenticated Pike or Mazzini collection. It is pinned at Charleston because that is where the legend locates Pike, not because anything happened there
stops.campa: A letter is said to exist in which Pike writes to Giuseppe Mazzini on the fifteenth of August 1871, laying out three world wars to be engineered in sequence, ending in the universal reign of Lucifer. It has a date, a sender, a recipient, and a famous repository. It has no shelfmark, no photograph, and no record of anyone having handled it. Its three-war script postdates the events it claims to foretell. William Guy Carr puts it into wide circulation in 1955 in Pawns in the Game, and it has been quoted for seventy years since; no authenticated Pike or Mazzini collection contains it.
suggested_refs: William Guy Carr, Pawns in the Game (1955), the popularizer of the alleged letter

stops.name: Paris, Leo Taxil confesses
stops.date_confidence: attested; the confession of 19 April 1897 is confirmed. The dossier names the venue as the Societe de Geographie; that hall is not confirmed by an independent source and the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: Gabriel Jogand-Pages, writing as Leo Taxil, has spent twelve years selling France an exposure of a Luciferian order called the Palladium, run from Charleston by Albert Pike, complete with a repentant priestess named Diana Vaughan. Priests and journalists come to a Paris hall on the nineteenth of April to meet her. Taxil tells them she never existed, that he wrote all of it, and that his own conversion to Catholicism was part of the joke. Then he leaves the hall. Pike has been dead six years, and the Palladium outlives the confession that invented it and is still in print.

stops.name: Judiciary Square, the monument in civilian bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested; authorized by Congress 9 April 1898 and dedicated 23 October 1901. Coordinate is 3rd and D Streets NW
stops.campa: Congress authorizes it in 1898 and Masons pay for it, and Gaetano Trentanove's bronze goes up at Third and D Streets in 1901: Pike in a frock coat with a book, the Goddess of Masonry below him holding the banner of the Rite. No uniform, no sword, no horse. It is a monument to the author and the Sovereign Grand Commander, put up by the order he ran, and for the next century it is the only outdoor statue of a Confederate military officer in the city of Washington.

stops.name: House of the Temple, the crypt
stops.date_confidence: attested; the remains were moved from Oak Hill on 29 December 1944. Coordinate is the canonical House of the Temple pin used in prince_hall.journey.json
stops.campa: John Russell Pope built the House of the Temple on 16th Street between 1911 and 1915, modeled on the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the seven wonders and a tomb. Twenty-nine years later the Supreme Council takes Pike out of Oak Hill and puts him in a crypt inside it, with his library and his manuscripts around him. The man asked to be burned and scattered, and is instead the only body in a replica of the most famous tomb in the ancient world. The remains are moved out of Oak Hill on the twenty-ninth of December 1944.

stops.name: Washington, the annotated edition
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 2011; day defaulted
stops.campa: The Southern Jurisdiction stopped giving out Morals and Dogma in 1969 and replaced it with commentaries and digests, on the reasonable grounds that nobody was reading it. In August 2011 its Grand Archivist, Arturo de Hoyos, publishes the whole thing again with roughly four thousand notes: sources identified, borrowings traced, paragraphs renumbered, headings restored from Pike's manuscripts. The better writers Pike said he had taken from are named in the margin at last. New members receive the book once more.
stops.quote: Every one is entirely free to reject and dissent from whatsoever herein may seem to him to be untrue or unsound.

stops.name: Judiciary Square, pulled down and burned
stops.date_confidence: attested; toppled and burned on the evening of 19 June 2020, wreckage removed by the National Park Service the following day
stops.campa: The D.C. Council petitioned for removal in 1992; there were calls after Charlottesville in 2017 and a relocation bill from Eleanor Holmes Norton in 2019, and none of them moved the statue. On Juneteenth, during the protests after the murder of George Floyd, demonstrators put ropes and chains on the bronze, pull it off its pedestal, pour accelerant over it, and set it alight. What brings them is the Klan office nobody has ever produced a document for, and the Confederate stars he certainly did wear. The Park Service hauls the wreckage away the next morning.
suggested_refs: The 1992 D.C. Council petition, the 2017 post-Charlottesville calls, and Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton's 2019 relocation bill

stops.name: Judiciary Square, set back up
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict on the day and neither could be checked against the National Park Service release, whose cited URL returns HTTP 404. Wikipedia gives 27 October 2025; the research pool's chronology gave 25 October. Read as late October 2025
stops.campa: The National Park Service conserves the statue and puts it back at Third and D Streets in late October 2025, following a presidential executive order on historic monuments. It is the same bronze, repaired, on the same pedestal, five years and four months after the burning. Whether Albert Pike was a Klan judicial officer no document has ever settled; that he negotiated nine treaties for the Confederacy and commanded Cherokee troops at Pea Ridge has never been in dispute. Which October day it went back up is unsettled too: Wikipedia gives the twenty-seventh, the research pool the twenty-fifth, and the Park Service release cited for it 404s.
